passage:
"Papa, the brochure says seventy percent of their students get into top colleges," said Gargi's younger brother, waving it.
"Seventy percent!" Yogesh said. "That's the school, then."
Gargi took the brochure. "Let's say it three ways. Seventy percent get in. Thirty percent don't. And in numbers: their batch last year was forty students, so twenty-eight got in and twelve didn't."
"Twelve didn't," Yogesh repeated slowly.
"The other school says sixty percent, but their batch was two hundred. That's a hundred and twenty students."
"So it depends how you say it."
"Exactly. I'm not saying which one. I just want us to see it straight before choosing."

qa.q: How many students were in the first school's batch last year?
qa.a: The first school's batch last year had forty students.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh repeat "Twelve didn't" slowly?
qa.a: Hearing the same result as a loss and in real numbers made it feel different from "seventy percent", and Yogesh was taking in the fuller picture.

qa.q: Why is Gargi's three-ways method fair?
qa.a: Saying the result as a gain, as a loss and in absolute numbers shows the full picture without pushing either school, so the family can choose clearly.

qa.q: How might the younger brother feel after Gargi's explanation?
qa.a: He may feel a little deflated that his exciting number lost its shine, but also clearer about what the brochures really say.

grounding: Shows a mature young adult restating a school choice as gain, as loss and in absolute numbers, framing it fairly rather than to steer the family.

passage: When I first became a project lead, I learned how easily I could steer people with words. I'm Ishita. We had to choose between two software vendors, and I preferred the cheaper one. My first draft of the email said, "Vendor A saves us 30%!" Then I remembered how I'd felt when Pranav once pitched something as "cuts risk by half" and I agreed without thinking. So I rewrote it: "Vendor A costs 30% less, about ₹4 lakh a year. It also has 20% more downtime, around three extra hours a month. Vendor B costs more and is steadier." Pranav read it and said, "I can't tell which one you like." That was the point. The team chose B, and I think they chose well.

qa.q: How much less does Vendor A cost per year?
qa.a: Vendor A costs 30% less, about ₹4 lakh a year.

qa.q: Why did Ishita remember Pranav's "cuts risk by half" pitch?
qa.a: Ishita felt uneasy remembering agreeing without thinking because of that wording, and didn't want to steer the team the same way.

qa.q: What made Ishita's rewritten email fair?
qa.a: It gave both the gain and the cost of each vendor in plain numbers, so the team could weigh them without being nudged by one shiny phrase.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel reading an email that hides Ishita's preference?
qa.a: Pranav may feel trusted to decide on the facts, and perhaps a little impressed that the email didn't try to sell anything.

grounding: Shows a young lead restating a choice as both gain and loss in absolute numbers and framing it fairly for others instead of steering them.

passage:
Supervisor's note, education NGO, Tuesday. Anand.
I watched Tarun, our youngest programme officer, speak to a room of parents about the new scholarship exam. The official poster says: "One in five students wins a scholarship!" Tarun didn't read it out. Instead he said, "Last year, 200 students took it. 40 won. 160 didn't. So it's worth trying, and it's also worth having a second plan." A few parents looked less excited, but more of them asked sensible questions: about fees if their child didn't win, about other schemes. One father told me afterwards it was the first time someone had given him the whole picture.
What I did: I asked Tarun to help us rewrite the poster the same way.

qa.q: How many students won the scholarship last year?
qa.a: Last year, 40 students won.

qa.q: Why did some parents look less excited after Tarun spoke?
qa.a: Hearing that 160 didn't win, not just "one in five", made the real odds clear, which dampened the excitement but helped them think.

qa.q: Why did Tarun's way of speaking lead to better questions?
qa.a: Giving the gain, the loss and the real numbers let parents plan for both outcomes, so they asked about fees and other schemes.

qa.q: How did the father who spoke to Anand experience Tarun's talk?
qa.a: He felt respected, saying it was the first time someone had given him the whole picture instead of a hopeful slogan. 🙏

grounding: Shows a young officer stating the scholarship odds as gain, loss and absolute numbers so parents can decide fairly rather than be steered.

passage:
14 March, late
Team vote tomorrow on the new rota. Ujjwal asked me to present the staff survey. First line of my draft: "75% of the team prefer four long days!" I liked how it sounded because I want this change too. Then I stopped and read it again.
Other side of the same survey: 25% don't want it. That's 9 of our 36 people, and I checked, most of them are the ones who pick up kids at five. "Seventy-five percent" hides nine actual faces.
So I rewrote the slide:
27 of 36 prefer four long days.
9 of 36 prefer the current five days, mainly for school pick-up.
Then I wrote down what I'd choose myself if the numbers were even. Still four days, but with a swap option.
I'd rather lose the vote than win it with a sentence that nudges people.
Parveen

qa.q: How many of the 36 people prefer the current five days?
qa.a: 9 of 36 prefer the current five days, mainly for school pick-up.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel uneasy about the first draft line?
qa.a: Parveen wanted the change too and noticed that '75% prefer' sounded like a clear win while hiding the nine real people who would be affected.

qa.q: What steps did Parveen take before deciding on a personal choice?
qa.a: Parveen restated the survey as both a gain and a loss, wrote it in plain counts out of 36, and then asked what the choice would be if the numbers were even.

qa.q: How might the nine staff who pick up their children at five see the new slide?
qa.a: They are likely to feel counted rather than brushed aside, since the slide shows their reason next to the majority view instead of hiding them inside a percentage.

grounding: It shows a mature person restating a choice as gain, as loss and in absolute counts before deciding, and presenting it fairly to others rather than steering them.

passage: At the panchayat meeting in a village near Wardha, the seed company's leaflet said the new cotton variety "reduces crop loss by 50 percent!" Everyone murmured. Madhav, the young agriculture officer, stood up with the leaflet. "Let's say it three ways before anyone decides. Fifty percent less loss sounds big. But on our fields, loss has been about four quintals out of a hundred. So this seed saves around two quintals. And the seed costs more, so some of you could still end up with less in hand if prices fall." Tarun, who farmed six acres, scratched his head. "So it's good, but not magic." "Good for some fields, magic for none," Madhav said. "I'll show my working to anyone who wants it. You decide."

qa.q: How much has loss been on their fields, according to Madhav?
qa.a: About four quintals out of a hundred.

qa.q: Why did Madhav stand up with the leaflet?
qa.a: He felt concerned that "50 percent less loss" would sound bigger than it was, and wanted the farmers to decide from fair numbers.

qa.q: How did Madhav frame the choice fairly?
qa.a: He restated it as a percentage, as actual quintals saved and as a possible downside if prices fall, then left the choice to the farmers.

qa.q: How does Tarun see the seed after Madhav speaks?
qa.a: Tarun sees it as good but not magic, a clearer picture than the leaflet gave.

grounding: A young officer restates a seed offer as gain, as loss and in plain quintals before farmers decide, rather than steering them.

passage: In the planning office in Oslo, Siddiq had two slides ready for the council. His manager's draft said, "The new crossing will cut accidents by 25 percent!" Siddiq added a line under it: "That means from about eight a year to about six." Then a second slide: "Put another way, even with the crossing we expect around six accidents a year. The cost is four months of roadworks outside the school." Astrid, a council member known for hard questions, read both slides. "Your manager's version sounded like a miracle," she said. "Yours sounds like a fair trade." "I want you to choose it for the right reasons," Siddiq said, "or turn it down for the right reasons." The council voted yes, and later nobody felt tricked.

qa.q: What does a 25 percent cut mean in accidents per year?
qa.a: From about eight a year to about six.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq add lines under his manager's slide?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about steering the council with a percentage that sounded like a miracle, and wanted them to see the real numbers and the cost.

qa.q: What makes Siddiq's slides a fair way to present a choice?
qa.a: They give the percentage, the plain numbers, what remains and the cost, so the council decides on the full picture.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Siddiq's version?
qa.a: Astrid sees it as a fair trade rather than a miracle, and seems to trust it more.

grounding: A young planner restates a benefit in plain numbers, as what remains and with its cost, so the council is not steered by one framing.

passage: The hostel committee had to choose between two mess caterers, and the notice Preeti found pinned up that morning said: "New caterer: 80% of students at St. Joseph's loved the food!" She took it down before the vote. At the meeting she wrote on the whiteboard instead: "At St. Joseph's, 80 out of 100 liked it; 20 out of 100 didn't. Our current caterer: 70 liked, 30 didn't. New one costs 300 more per month." Mridul, the mess secretary, frowned. "The old notice was more exciting." "It was written to make us vote one way," Preeti said. "I'd rather we choose knowing both sides." The vote was close. The new caterer won, and nobody complained later that they'd been sold something.

qa.q: How many out of 100 at St. Joseph's didn't like the new caterer's food?
qa.a: 20 out of 100.

qa.q: Why did Preeti take the notice down before the vote?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable with a notice written to push the vote one way, and wanted everyone to choose knowing both sides.

qa.q: How did Preeti's whiteboard make the choice fairer?
qa.a: It showed who liked and disliked each caterer in plain numbers, plus the extra cost, instead of one exciting percentage.

qa.q: How does Mridul react to Preeti's version?
qa.a: Mridul finds the old notice more exciting, but the fair version meant nobody felt sold something later.

grounding: A young woman replaces a one-sided notice with both likes and dislikes in plain numbers so others can choose fairly.

passage:
Subject: Before we send the canteen proposal
Hi Lokesh,
I read your draft for the committee. It's clear, but I think it steers them. For Anna's Kitchen you wrote "only 5% complaints," and for the current caterer "complaints in 1 of every 12 meals." The numbers aren't far apart, but the second sounds much worse.
When I made the choice for myself last night, I wrote each option three ways: meals that went fine, meals with a complaint, and the actual count out of the 600 meals we served last month. Anna's Kitchen: 570 fine, 30 complaints. Current caterer: 550 fine, 50 complaints. Written like that, the gap is real but modest, and I still lean to Anna's Kitchen.
Could we put the same three lines for both in the proposal and let the committee decide?
Lalit

qa.q: How many meals were served last month, according to Lalit's email?
qa.a: 600 meals were served last month.

qa.q: What worries Lalit about Lokesh's draft?
qa.a: Lalit is uneasy that the draft steers the committee, making one caterer sound much worse through wording rather than numbers.

qa.q: What does Lalit suggest, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Putting the same three lines, fine meals, complaints and counts out of 600, for both caterers, so the committee decides on facts rather than framing.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Lokesh might feel a little defensive at first, but also relieved to get a clear, respectful way to fix the draft.

grounding: Shows a mature colleague restating both options as gains, losses and counts before deciding, and asking that the committee see a fair frame.

passage: Thanks, Disha. So, I'm Kalyani, and two years into the job the ward office asked me to present a change: garbage pickup every other day instead of daily, with separate bins. My boss wanted me to lead with "We save forty percent of truck trips!" And honestly, that line excited me. Then I wrote it the other way: "Your lane goes without pickup three days a week." That one made me flinch. So I wrote a third version in plain numbers: ten truck trips a week become six, and each lane gets four pickups a week instead of seven. Looking at all three, I still thought it was worth trying, but I understood why people might hate it. At the residents' meeting I put all three lines on one slide. A few people shouted. But nobody could say I tricked them, and the vote was theirs.

qa.q: What change did the ward office ask Kalyani to present?
qa.a: Garbage pickup every other day instead of daily, with separate bins.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when writing the change as a loss?

qa.q: What did Kalyani put on the slide, and why was that fair?
qa.a: The gain, the loss and the plain numbers together, so residents could judge the change without being steered.

qa.q: How might the residents who shouted see the meeting?
qa.a: They were still unhappy about fewer pickups, but they could see the full picture and knew the vote was theirs.

grounding: Shows a young professional stating a change as gain, loss and absolute numbers before deciding, and presenting it fairly rather than steering residents.

passage: I was the one holding the map when Sonali called the group together at the tea stall below the pass. Two ways up: the ridge path or the valley road. She didn't say which she liked. passage:
Monday. Keerthana, the new coordinator at a Hyderabad school, got a pitch from a vendor for a new attendance system. The brochure said: "Cuts late arrivals by 30%!" Afreen, her colleague, was excited. "Thirty percent! Let's do it."

Wednesday. Keerthana asked the vendor for real numbers. At a school like theirs, late arrivals went from about ten students a day to seven. Out of four hundred. She wrote it both ways on a sheet: "Cuts late arrivals by 30%." "Three fewer late students a day, out of 400." Then a third line: "Costs the same as two new projectors."

Friday. She presented to the principal. She showed all three lines, gain and cost, percent and absolute. "I don't want to push you either way," she said. "Here's what it looks like from every side."

The principal read it twice. "Thank you. The brochure made it sound huge."

Afreen said later, "I'd have bought it on Monday."

qa.q: What did the brochure claim?
qa.a: Cuts late arrivals by 30%!

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she presented all three lines?
qa.a: Keerthana felt calm and careful, wanting to be fair and not steer the principal either way.

qa.q: How did Keerthana's reframing help the decision?
qa.a: By restating the claim in absolute numbers and next to its cost, Keerthana showed the real size of the gain so the principal could judge fairly.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the decision after Friday?
qa.a: Afreen seems a little embarrassed but grateful, realising Afreen would have bought it on Monday because of the percentage.

grounding: Over a week, a coordinator restates a vendor's claim as gain, loss and absolute numbers, and presents it fairly.

passage:
Arohi, you want to tell your team the new rota is "much better"? Hmm. Sit. Your Seema aunty learned something about this long ago.

When I was twenty-five, I was the panchayat secretary in our village near Nashik. We had to change the water supply timings. The new plan gave every lane water for two hours, but in the evening instead of the morning.

The sarpanch wanted me to announce: "Everyone gets two full hours!" I knew that was only half. For the women who fetched water before work, evening meant losing the morning.

So I wrote it both ways on the notice. "What you gain: two hours, every day, same for every lane. What you lose: morning water. Old: one and a half hours. New: two hours."

Some people were angry. But nobody felt tricked. And a month later, the lanes agreed to a trial with one morning hour.

So, beta, what does your team lose?

qa.q: How long did the new plan give every lane water?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What did young Seema feel about the sarpanch's announcement?
qa.a: Young Seema felt uneasy, knowing it told only half the story and would feel like a trick to the women losing morning water.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Seema's story?
qa.a: Writing the notice with both gains and losses, and old and new hours, meant people felt informed, not tricked, which led to a fair trial later.

qa.q: How might the women who fetched water before work have felt reading the notice?
qa.a: They may have felt upset about losing morning water, but respected because it was stated honestly.

grounding: An elder recalls restating a water plan as both gain and loss, in plain numbers, rather than framing it to steer people.

passage:
The power had gone out at the Bhopal warehouse, and Rafiq had until five to send his manager, Asif, a proposal for new shift timings. Laptop battery at thirty percent.

He'd already written the first line: "New shifts will reduce overtime by 25%!" It sounded great. He hovered over send.

Then he stopped. Would the workers read it that way? What they'd lose was the Saturday half-day. And what did twenty-five percent mean in hours?

He rewrote it quickly, by the light of the window. "Gain: overtime drops from 8 hours a week to 6, on average. Loss: Saturday half-day becomes a full day once a month. Same pay."

It looked less exciting. But it was true from every side.

At 4:40, he sent it. Asif called back an hour later. "This is clear. The union will trust it more too."

Rafiq exhaled. He'd nearly sent a sales pitch instead of a proposal.

qa.q: How much would overtime drop per week, in hours?
qa.a: From 8 hours a week to 6, on average.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling as he hovered over send?
qa.a: Rafiq felt tempted by the exciting line but then uneasy, realising the workers might feel misled.

qa.q: How did Rafiq reframe the proposal, and why was it fairer?
qa.a: Rafiq restated the change as hours gained and lost, in absolute numbers, so readers could judge it themselves instead of being steered.

qa.q: How might Asif and the union see Rafiq's proposal?
qa.a: Asif and the union are likely to trust it more because it shows both gains and losses clearly.

grounding: Under a deadline and power cut, a young worker restates a proposal as gains, losses and absolute hours rather than a steering claim.

passage: Yusuf had already typed the notice for the Lakeview Apartments group chat: "Solar panels will CUT our common electricity bill by 30%!!" He showed it to Farhan in the lift. Farhan read it twice. "True," he said, "but it's half the picture." That evening in the society office, Farhan wrote three lines on the whiteboard. Gain: the common bill falls by about thirty percent. Loss: each flat pays four thousand once, and the roof garden shrinks. Plain numbers: roughly nine thousand saved a month across forty flats, so the cost is covered in about eighteen months. "Let people see all three," Farhan said. Yusuf frowned. "Fewer will say yes." "Then the yes will mean something." Yusuf sighed, deleted the exclamation marks, and pasted the three lines into the chat instead.

qa.q: How much would each flat pay once for the solar panels?
qa.a: Each flat pays four thousand once.

qa.q: What does Farhan seem to feel about Yusuf's notice?
qa.a: Farhan seems calm but uneasy with it, feeling it is true but one-sided, and wanting neighbours to decide with the whole picture.

qa.q: Which choice made the decision fairer, and why?
qa.a: Writing the gain, the loss and the plain numbers side by side, because residents could weigh the real trade-off instead of being steered by one bright line.

qa.q: Why might Yusuf react differently to the whiteboard than Farhan?
qa.a: Yusuf is keen to get the panels approved and worries that showing the cost will mean fewer yes votes, so the full picture feels like a risk.

grounding: Shows a mature person restating a choice as gain, as loss and in absolute numbers, and framing it fairly for others instead of steering them.
